newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: Top aide to N.Korea's Kim seeks asylum in South.
newsitem.headline: Top aide to N.Korea's Kim seeks asylum in South.

text.p: Two North Korean officials, including a top aide to North Korean leader Kim Jong-il, are seeking asylum in South Korea, the Seoul Foreign Ministry said on Wednesday.

Hwang Jang-yop, a secretary in the communist nation's ruling Workers' Party and a member of its central committee, and his assistant Kim Dok-hong sought asylum at the South Korean embassy in the Chinese capital Beijing, it said.

"Workers' Party secretary Hwang Jang-yop expressed intention to defect at 10:05 a.m. (0205 GMT) at the consular section of the embassy," Ryu Kwang-sok, director-general of the Foreign Ministry's Asia-Pacific Bureau, told reporters.

Ryu said Hwang, the highest ranking North Korean official to seek asylum in the capitalist South, had been picked by the North Korean leader to formulate the Stalinist state's juche, or self-reliance, ideology.

Hwang, 73, is one of 11 secretaries on the powerful secretariat of the Workers' Party. The secretariat includes Kim Jong-il, the son and political heir of North Korean founder Kim Il-sung who died in July 1994.
Kim Jong-il, who has been ruling the North since his father's death, has yet to take over top posts as state president and general-secretary of the ruling party.
Hwang's defection comes only four days before the younger Kim's 55th birthday, described by Pyongyang as the most important holiday.
"Our embassy in China has notified Hwang's defection to the Chinese authorities and we are trying to resolve the matter through diplomatic channels," Ryu said.

South Korean Foreign Minister Yoo Chong-ha cancelled his scheduled visit to Singapore to attend a meeting of European and Southeast Asian officials to concentrate on diplomatic efforts to bring Hwang to Seoul, he added.
The exact reason for Hwang's defection is being investigated, he said.
A string of officials from the impoverished North have defected to South Korea in recent years, including diplomats, air force pilots and foreign exchange dealers.
North Korea, whose economy has contracted in the past six years, has been suffering from an acute food shortage in the past two years, due partly to devastating floods.
Ryu said Hwang went to the South Korean embassy after his two-week visit to Japan.
Hwang's visit to Japan had caused concern in South Korea that Tokyo might be taking steps to improve ties with the communist nation.
Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto told South Korean President Kim Young-sam at a meeting in a Japan resort last month that Japanese government officials would not meet Hwang.
Japan, which has a large ethnic Korean population, has diplomatic ties with South Korea, but not with North Korea.
